nodes.label: Performance is conversion: 31% better LCP → +8% sales (Vodafone A/B)
nodes.source_location: section: Performance is conversion: 31% better LCP → +8% sales (Vodafone A/B)
nodes.rationale: You can raise conversion before opening Figma — web performance is a conversion lever, not an engineering nicety. Vodafone Italy A/B tested web-vitals optimization (LCP 31% better than control, same offer/creative/screen, 100k clicks and 34k visits/day per variant, paid traffic): +8% sales, +15% lead-to-visit, +11% cart-to-visit.

nodes.label: Compliments aren't validation — "what's missing for you to PIX now?" is
nodes.source_location: section: Compliments aren't validation — "what's missing for you to PIX now?" is
nodes.rationale: Everyone loves your idea, nobody bought. Compliments are free and worth nothing (like your freemium). The simplest validation test: try to sell. If you can't close inside your ICP, ask directly: "Falta o que pra você fazer o PIX agora?" ("What's missing for you to send the PIX instant payment right now?") The pause reveals the truth — either the real objection (your build list) or excuses (the "loved it" was just politeness). Follow up: "If it had that, would you pay now?" Then do 20 sales this way.

nodes.label: "Paint the button" is judging the last line of a long cascade
nodes.source_location: section: "Paint the button" is judging the last line of a long cascade
nodes.rationale: The visual layer of a landing page is the tip of a cascade that begins at the ICP — so "make it more colorful" critiques the *end* of a process as if it were the start.

nodes.label: Scaling cold traffic is an honesty test for your page
nodes.source_location: section: Scaling cold traffic is an honesty test for your page
nodes.rationale: Conversion measured on warm audiences (existing followers) is inflated — they forgive the page's flaws. Only cold traffic reveals how much of your rate is the page versus borrowed trust.

nodes.label: Test hero comprehension with a stranger from your ICP
nodes.source_location: section: Test hero comprehension with a stranger from your ICP
nodes.rationale: The cheapest usability test nobody runs: show your LP hero to one person for 5 seconds, take it away, ask "What does this product do? For whom?" If they can't answer, the hero failed — no matter how pretty it is. In those seconds the brain asks three questions, almost in order: what is this → is this for me → why should I care now. The mechanism is cognitive load: every second spent decoding what you do is a second closer to giving up — clarity beats cleverness at the top of the funnel, always.

nodes.label: Write the CTA microcopy, not the button color
nodes.source_location: section: Write the CTA microcopy, not the button color
nodes.rationale: The CTA label moves conversion far more than button color or shape — it's the last thing the user reads before deciding, so it must reduce the mental effort of simulating what happens next.

nodes.label: Cut CAC by filtering on the landing page, not the media
nodes.source_location: section: Cut CAC by filtering on the landing page, not the media
nodes.rationale: High CAC is rarely a media problem — it's usually a filtering problem. The landing page can qualify leads before the form, killing deals that were never going to close.

nodes.label: Aim for 4.2–4.5 stars, not a perfect 5
nodes.source_location: section: Aim for 4.2–4.5 stars, not a perfect 5
nodes.rationale: A flawless rating reads as fake; consumers distrust unanimity. A profile that includes constructive criticism feels more authentic and converts better than pure praise.

nodes.label: Compress the decision window — shorten the path to action below the path to doubt
nodes.source_location: section: Compress the decision window — shorten the path to action below the path to doubt
nodes.rationale: The purchase decision is mostly made before checkout. Conversion is architecture: the user converts when the path to the action is shorter than the path to doubt, because every extra second of deliberation raises the odds they close the tab.

nodes.label: Don't clone the page — the converting layer is invisible
nodes.source_location: section: Don't clone the page — the converting layer is invisible
nodes.rationale: A converting sales page is the visible shell of an invisible system. Copying the layout copies what's cheapest to produce; the expensive part (research) stays invisible and gets left behind.

nodes.label: Pass the 5-second test — lead with the problem, not the feature
nodes.source_location: section: Pass the 5-second test — lead with the problem, not the feature
nodes.rationale: A visitor scans your LP for ~5 seconds. If they can't answer what it does, who it's for, and why they should care, they leave — they won't stay to figure it out. Conversion begins on the first line.

nodes.label: Fix contrast, layout, and trust before rewriting copy
nodes.source_location: section: Fix contrast, layout, and trust before rewriting copy
nodes.rationale: The brain processes three pre-verbal variables — contrast, on-screen placement, and trust — before it reads the words, and they usually move the needle more than any headline.

nodes.label: Specificity is the difference between decoration and persuasion
nodes.source_location: section: Specificity is the difference between decoration and persuasion
nodes.rationale: Generic LP copy gets discarded by the brain; specific messages are processed faster and generate more trust. A converting LP shows the *transformation* the product causes, not just what it does.

nodes.label: Users scan, they don't read — give the primary action obvious contrast
nodes.source_location: section: Users scan, they don't read — give the primary action obvious contrast
nodes.rationale: Users scan interfaces, weighing cognitive effort against payoff, and ignore most of it. They enter with one question — "What can I do here?" — so the primary action must win on contrast within seconds.

nodes.label: Judge a landing page by conversion, not by beauty
nodes.source_location: section: Judge a landing page by conversion, not by beauty
nodes.rationale: A landing page isn't a beauty contest — it has one measurable job: qualify the user and lower CAC by turning traffic into revenue. Evaluating a static image with no context is nearly useless.

nodes.label: Converting pages are often ugly — design for performance, not applause
nodes.source_location: section: Converting pages are often ugly — design for performance, not applause
nodes.rationale: There's an invisible war between branding (looking good in the screenshot) and performance (conversion, retention, expansion). The page that puts money in the till is often visually aggressive, text-heavy, and far from the Apple aesthetic founders dream of.

nodes.label: Design the features page for skimming, not reading
nodes.source_location: section: Design the features page for skimming, not reading
nodes.rationale: Almost nobody reads your features page — they skim three bullets and hunt for a demo video. Design for that behavior (with the caveat that the more conscious, technical slice of your ICP *will* read the detail).

nodes.label: No clicks out, plus brutal CTA contrast
nodes.source_location: section: No clicks out, plus brutal CTA contrast
nodes.rationale: For conversion you want little distraction and lots of redundancy. Any clickable element that leads off-page is lost conversion — no matter how prestigious the source.

nodes.label: Debug ICP and awareness level before touching design
nodes.source_location: section: Debug ICP and awareness level before touching design
nodes.rationale: Conversion is context engineering — who arrives, with what pain, at what stage, needing what proof. Two invisible variables must be debugged before writing a line of code: the Who (ICP) and the When (awareness level). Visual design comes last.

nodes.label: The 2026 landing page checklist
nodes.rationale: An all-in-one checklist for a converting LP — @namyakhann's (Supafast) list, which Richard translated and endorsed in full: Hero (1 clear promise / 1 specific audience / 1 exact-action CTA / show-don't-explain visual / trust seal above the fold). Copy (headline <10 words, benefit before feature, customer language, one central transformation, scannable in 5s). Social proof (logos if you have names, metrics if you have traction, specific result testimonials, zero generic praise). Structure (Hero → Pain → Solution → Proof → CTA; max 3 feature sections; FAQ kills top 5 objections; CTA repeated 2–3x). Technical (<3s load, real mobile-first, single-scroll flow).

nodes.label: Click triggers: one line of risk-reducing microcopy next to the CTA
nodes.source_location: section: Click triggers: one line of risk-reducing microcopy next to the CTA
nodes.rationale: A single line of text reducing perceived risk can save conversion — in CRO these are "click triggers" (marketing calls it objection-breaking): "Lifetime guarantee," "Free shipping," "7 days free, no card." It's certainty placed on top of a known ICP doubt.

nodes.label: Founder LP guide: platform doesn't matter, load time does; proof must outweigh the promise
nodes.source_location: section: Founder LP guide: platform doesn't matter, load time does; proof must outweigh the promise
nodes.rationale: Profits are more sensitive to conversions than to costs, and the landing page is often the first gate between a founder's product and its users. The platform matters less than speed, clarity, contrast, proof, and direct action.

nodes.label: Match CTA microcopy to the funnel stage
nodes.source_location: section: Match CTA microcopy to the funnel stage
nodes.rationale: Button text should change with the user's progress in the funnel — the verb matches the mental state at each stage. First interaction: "Descubra como funciona" ("See how it works"). Product page: "Quero esse produto" ("I want this product"). Checkout: "Finalizar minha compra" ("Complete my purchase"). Short (≤4 words), clear, directional. This discreet personalization raises perceived control, confidence, and conversion.

nodes.label: Real humans outconvert models — banner blindness explains why
nodes.source_location: section: Real humans outconvert models — banner blindness explains why
nodes.rationale: Highrise, the 37signals CRM, tested homepage variants with different human figures; real users and actual team developers converted best on average — above stock-photo models. (37signals later became Basecamp.) Likely explanation: banner blindness — we learn to ignore what looks like advertising and give attention to what's organic or unusual.
